newsitem.title: USA: U.S. analysts applaud Mexico's early loan payment.
newsitem.headline: U.S. analysts applaud Mexico's early loan payment.

text.p: Mexico's early repayment of the emergency loan to the U.S. Treasury is a declaration of financial solvency and independence as it officially puts an end to the 1995 peso crisis, U.S. analysts said.
"It shows Mexico is serious about its stabilization program and has regained access to the market to borrow money," said Thomas Trebat, head of emerging market research at Citicorp Securities.

Mexican Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz announced the country would immediately repay the outstanding $3.5 billion of a loan from the U.S. Treasury and would also repay early $1.5 billion owed to the International Monetary Fund.

Mexico's export performance improved last year, thanks partly to rising oil revenues. But Trebat said export earnings probably contributed little to the repayment. He noted that the country's current account is roughly in balance.
Instead, the repayment is part of a refinancing operation. Mexico borrowed from international capital market to pay down the debt owed to the U.S. Treasury and the IMF.
Ortiz said this operation could save Mexcio $100 million in interest payments.

Even bigger savings will come from lower principal payments, said Lawrence Goodman, head of Latin America research at Salomon Brothers. Access to the international market and adept liability management could save Mexico $1.5 billion on principal payments, as it replaced payments due in 1998-2000 with longer dated debt, Goodman said.
"The real luster is wrapped up in the principal savings," he said.

Despite claims by the Mexican authorities that all the tesobonos -- short-term Mexican Treasury bills -- were paid off, investors perceived that the problem was still present in the form of borrowing from the U.S., he said.
By extinguishing the debt to the U.S. Treasury, the Mexican government finally took off the stigma the tesobono crisis, Goodman said.
"A more rational debt profile would reduce volatility of Mexcian interest rates and give the authroties greater access to the international market," he said.
Salomon Brothers was one of the co-lead managers of Mexico's $1 billion 10-year global bond issued last week.
Citicorp's Trebat said easing credit retraint would make it easier for Mexican corporations to tap the global capital market.

In the near term, the repayment would have scant impact on Mexico's overall indebtedness or the weight of dollar debt in its sovereign obligations, said Carlos Ansilis, senior Latin America economists at Oppenheimer and Co., Inc.
Loans owed to IMF would take much longer to pay back, but Mexcico is negotiating to secure an extended fund facility (EFF) to amortize over a longer period of time, he said.
Mexican officials said they would still owe the IMF $10 billion after this.
Even so, the consolidation of Mexican debt would be viewed favorably by investors.
"It is symbolic," Asilis said. "But symbolism is important."
Competent liability management would enhance Mexico's chance to get a credit upgrade, he said.
Many analysts and traders expect Mexicothat Mexico's sovereign credit rating to be raised a notch from the current BB by Standard and Poor's and Ba2 by Moody's Invenstors Service.
"What is holding back is upgrade is Mexico's weak banking sector," Asilis said.
Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers told reporters after Mexico announced the repayment that Mexico's banking system still faced strains despite the progress made.
